exercises.prompt: A film-restoration studio in Mumbai needs storage for three things: (1) the data directory of the PostgreSQL server that tracks its projects; (2) a directory of shared scripts and reference frames that 40 rendering machines mount at the same time; (3) 300 TB of finished, rarely changed video masters that partners download over HTTPS. Which storage kinds fit best, in that order?

options.label: block, file, object
options.feedback: Yes. A database wants a low-latency disk of its own; many machines sharing a directory want a network file system; large, write-once media for download want object storage.

options.label: object, block, file
options.feedback: Not yet — a database cannot run on an HTTP object API, and a block volume is normally attached to one machine at a time, not forty.

options.label: file, object, block
options.feedback: Not yet — 40 machines cannot all mount one block volume as a normal disk, and serving 300 TB to partners over HTTPS is exactly what object stores do.

options.label: object, object, object
options.feedback: Object storage is right for (3), but the database needs block-level reads and writes at any offset, and the render nodes need a shared POSIX file system with directories and locks.

hints: Ask of each: how many machines use it at once, and what interface does the software expect — a disk, a directory or HTTP?
exercises.solution: (1) A database engine reads and writes small pieces of its files at arbitrary offsets with low latency and expects a local file system on a disk: **block** storage. (2) Forty machines mounting the same directory need a shared file system over NFS or SMB: **file** storage. (3) Large, rarely changing objects fetched over HTTPS, at a low price per gigabyte and with high durability: **object** storage, perhaps with a lifecycle rule moving old masters to a cheaper class.

exercises.prompt: A national library stores 500 million objects in an object store with a designed annual durability of eleven nines (a probability of $10^{-11}$ of losing a given object in a year, independently). On average, how many **years** pass between losses of a single object?

feedback.message: Not yet — think about the expected number lost per year first, then invert it.
Not yet — check the powers of ten: $5 \times 10^8 \times 10^{-11} = 5 \times 10^{-3}$.

hints: Expected objects lost per year = number of objects × probability per object.
If 0.005 objects are lost per year, how many years per lost object?
exercises.solution: Expected losses per year are $5 \times 10^{8} \times 10^{-11} = 5 \times 10^{-3}$, so on average one object is lost every $1 / 0.005 = 200$ years. That is a statement about the provider's hardware under the model's assumptions; it does not cover deletion by the library's own software or staff, which is why versioning and backups are still needed.

exercises.prompt: A storage cluster protects data with a $(12, 4)$ erasure code: every object is split into 12 data fragments, 4 parity fragments are added, and any 12 of the 16 suffice to rebuild it. How many TB of raw disk does it need to store 600 TB of data (ignoring metadata)?

feedback.message: Not yet — that is three-way replication. An erasure code stores only $(k+m)/k$ bytes per byte.
Not yet — the code does not store 4 extra copies; it stores 4 extra *fragments*, each a twelfth of the object.

hints: Each object becomes 16 fragments, each $1/12$ of its size.
exercises.solution: Each byte becomes $16/12 = 4/3$ bytes on disk, so 600 TB needs $600 \times 4/3 = 800$ TB, and survives the loss of any 4 fragments of each object. Three-way replication of the same data would need 1800 TB and survive only 2 losses. The price is in repairs: rebuilding one fragment reads 12 others.

exercises.prompt: A storage service promises 99.9% availability per month. In a 30-day month, how many **seconds** of unavailability can occur before the promise is broken?

feedback.message: Close — that is the answer in minutes (43.2). The question asks for seconds.
Not yet — 99.9% leaves 0.1% of the month, not 0.01%.

exercises.solution: $30 \times 86{,}400 = 2{,}592{,}000$ seconds, and 0.1% of that is $2{,}592$ seconds — about 43 minutes. Compare durability: the same service may be designed to lose a given object with probability $10^{-11}$ a year. Availability nines and durability nines measure different things and are rarely equal.

exercises.prompt: A clinic-booking service in Bogotá takes a database snapshot every 6 hours (at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00) and keeps no change log. At 17:40 a faulty migration corrupts the database. The team restores the 12:00 snapshot and the service is working again at 19:10. What recovery point and recovery time did they actually achieve?

options.label: Data lost: 5 h 40 min of changes; out of service: 1 h 30 min
options.feedback: Yes. Everything after 12:00 is lost (to 17:40), and the service was down from 17:40 to 19:10.

options.label: Data lost: 6 h; out of service: 7 h 10 min
options.feedback: Not yet — the recovery point is measured to the moment of the disaster (17:40), and the recovery time from the disaster, not from the snapshot.

options.label: Data lost: 1 h 30 min; out of service: 5 h 40 min
options.feedback: Not yet — these are swapped. Lost data runs from the last good copy to the disaster; downtime runs from the disaster to recovery.

options.label: No data lost, because the snapshot was restored
options.feedback: Not yet — the snapshot is from 12:00; every booking made between 12:00 and 17:40 is gone unless it can be recovered some other way.

hints: The recovery point is the age of the copy you restored, measured at the moment of the disaster.
The recovery time runs from the disaster until service works again.
exercises.solution: Data from 12:00 to 17:40 is lost: **5 h 40 min**, the achieved recovery point. The service was out from 17:40 to 19:10: **1 h 30 min**, the achieved recovery time. With snapshots every 6 hours and no change log, the worst case is nearly 6 hours of lost bookings; archiving the database's change log every few minutes (point-in-time recovery) would have allowed restoring to 17:39, with a longer restore while the log is replayed.

exercises.prompt: A company's managed database has a synchronous standby in a second zone and an asynchronous replica in another region. An engineer accidentally runs `DELETE FROM orders;` without a `WHERE` clause on the primary. Which of these will let the company get its orders back?

options.label: Failing over to the standby in the second zone
options.feedback: Not yet — the standby is synchronous: it applied the delete at the same moment as the primary.

options.label: Promoting the replica in the other region
options.feedback: Not yet — asynchronous replication delays the delete by seconds at most; by the time anyone notices, the replica has applied it too.

options.label: Point-in-time recovery to just before the statement, from backups and the archived change log
options.feedback: Yes. Backups are copies from the past, so they can restore the table as it was a moment before the mistake.

options.label: Nothing: the provider's eleven nines of durability mean the data cannot be lost
options.feedback: Not yet — durability protects against hardware failure. A delete is a valid instruction from you, and the storage carries it out faithfully.

hints: What does each replica do with every change the primary makes — including a bad one?
exercises.solution: Replicas exist to stay identical to the primary, so they copy the mistaken delete within milliseconds (the synchronous standby) or seconds (the cross-region replica). Only a copy from the **past** helps: restore the most recent backup to a new instance and replay the archived change log up to just before the `DELETE` (point-in-time recovery), then copy the missing rows back. Replicas give availability; backups give recovery. You need both.

exercises.prompt: A language-learning app in Hanoi sends all writes to its database's primary and all reads to two asynchronous read replicas, to spread the load. Users report that after they change their daily goal, the settings page sometimes still shows the old goal, and shows the new one if they reload a few seconds later. Which change fixes this with the least extra load on the primary?

options.label: Route a user's reads to the primary for a short window (say 5 seconds) after that user writes, or read only from a replica that has applied the user's last write position
options.feedback: Yes — this gives read-your-writes (session) consistency for the user who wrote, while all other reads still go to the replicas.

options.label: Send every read to the primary
options.feedback: It works, but it gives up the read replicas entirely and puts all the read load back on the primary.

options.label: Add a third read replica
options.feedback: Not yet — another asynchronous replica has the same lag, so stale reads continue.

options.label: Make the client retry the read until the value changes
options.feedback: Not yet — the client cannot know whether the value *should* change (another device may have written something else), and retries add load and delay.

hints: The problem is replication lag between the primary and the replicas. Who needs to see the new value immediately — everyone, or the user who changed it?
exercises.solution: The users are seeing replication lag: the replica serving their read has not yet applied their write. They need **read-your-writes**, a session guarantee, not strong consistency for everyone. Two standard ways: send a user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after they write (sized from the measured lag distribution, including its tail), or return the write's log position to the client and read only from a replica that has reached it. Some services expose this directly as a *session* consistency level.

exercises.prompt:
The simplest erasure code adds one parity block: the byte-by-byte XOR of $k$ equal-length data blocks. It survives the loss of any one block. Write `xor_parity(blocks)`, which returns that parity as `bytes`, and `rebuild(blocks, parity)`, which receives the data blocks with exactly one replaced by `None` and returns a **new** list with the lost block recomputed. Do not modify the list you are given.

The starter's functions do not compute anything yet.
exercises.starter:
def xor_parity(blocks):
    """The byte-by-byte XOR of equal-length blocks (bytes objects)."""
    return blocks[0]                  # not yet: combine every block

def rebuild(blocks, parity):
    """blocks: the data blocks, with exactly one replaced by None (lost).
    Return a new list with the lost block recomputed from the others and the parity."""
    return list(blocks)               # not yet: the lost block is still None
exercises.tests:
blocks = [b"Kenya-01", b"Chile-02", b"Nepal-03", b"Ghana-04"]
p = xor_parity(blocks)
assert isinstance(p, bytes) and len(p) == 8
assert xor_parity([b"\x0f\xf0", b"\xff\x00"]) == b"\xf0\xf0"
assert xor_parity([b"abc"]) == b"abc", "the parity of one block is the block itself"
for lost in range(4):
    damaged = list(blocks)
    damaged[lost] = None
    fixed = rebuild(damaged, p)
    assert fixed == blocks, f"losing block {lost}: got {fixed}"
    assert damaged[lost] is None, "do not modify the list you were given"
# XOR of all blocks AND the parity is all zeros: that is the invariant the rebuild uses.
assert xor_parity(blocks + [p]) == bytes(8)
hints: XOR is its own inverse: $a \oplus b \oplus b = a$.
The XOR of all data blocks and the parity is all zeros, so the lost block equals the XOR of the surviving blocks and the parity.
Build the result in a `bytearray` and convert it with `bytes(...)` at the end.
